linkedin.about: Hi, I’m Raj. ​Some people meditate for peace, I ask questions. Basically, my work is to meet the smartest people and get into their minds. Not literally. I talk to them to learn from their expertise, their choices, and their life. And I take my viewers along for the ride. For me, figuring out money, business, health, relationships, and life was so confusing in the beginning, and I’m sure so many others face the same problem. But it gets a little bit easier when you have the right people sharing their lessons (and occasional disasters). When I’m not doing that, I’m hanging out with my dog, Crypto, who, unlike the real crypto, never disappoints me. Stick around to find out more about my experiences while doing all this.

When do you want to retire? 

Scroll for a few minutes and the feed answers for you, a guy who sold his startup at thirty, a girl explaining how to walk away before forty. 

Gen Z expects to retire around fifty-four on average, against seventy-one for their grandparents, and more than half say they belong to a movement built around leaving work as early as they can. 

Ask what they are chasing, and it is rarely a title or a company or a mark left on the world. It is time, freedom, a life they get to live while they are still young enough to feel it.

How do you tell whether a business idea will actually make money?

Asish Mohapatra, who built OfBusiness into one of the rare startups that made money while it scaled, has a test he runs on every new idea. 

He sets it a few very easy targets to hit in its first days: a day-one mark, a day-two mark, a day-three mark, all deliberately small. If the idea misses two, maybe three of them, he treats it as a bad idea and lets it go.

What does it cost to own a private jet?

In our recent episode, Abhinav Tripathi, Founder of JR Airlines & Private Jet Operator, said that keeping a single jet running comes to around ₹25 crore a year before it earns you anything back. 

Every trip, the plane flies empty to come get you, flies you where you're going, then flies empty again to get back or reach its next customer, so you're paying for far more air time than the hours you're on board.

Health is one of those areas for me. I have seen health issues closely in my family, and it showed me how long a problem can sit inside someone before anyone knows it is there. That is a big reason I invested in Neko Health a few months ago. Neko helps people understand what is happening inside their body before something becomes serious, collecting millions of health data points in a single visit and then sitting them down with a clinician who explains what matters. In the outcome data it has shared, around 1% of people with no symptoms had a severe, potentially life-threatening condition found, including heart problems and skin cancers they had no idea about. I looked at the business, the product, the market and the team the way I would with any company, and the conviction came from understanding the problem the moment I saw it. When I back a company, I usually look for three things: a very large problem, a shift in behaviour that feels inevitable, and some personal understanding of why the problem matters. Most investing advice tells you to stay detached and let market size, growth and returns make the decision. Those things matter, and an investor can back good companies without living every problem they invest in. But when a problem is personal, you understand what it costs the people living with it in a way no market report can show you. The investments I hold closest are the companies I would want to exist even if I had no stake in them. In our recent episode, part of the Mobius Foundation sustainability dialogue series, Sumant Sinha , the Founder, Chairman & CEO of ReNew , explained why the US keeps leaning into fossil fuels while much of the world pushes toward clean energy. A country's energy policy follows the money. The US is sitting on an enormous, profitable fossil fuel business, so doubling down on oil and gas makes economic sense for them. A lot of the global energy debate runs on this, each country defending the energy source it already profits from. Sinha's bigger argument is that this comfort is a trap. As the world electrifies more of everything, from cars to factories to AI data centres, the advantage shifts to whoever can produce cheap, clean power at scale. The countries building that capacity now are setting up to hold the leverage later, the way oil-rich countries have held it for the last century. posts.caption:
One bad conversation doesn’t define your relationships.
One rejection doesn’t define your potential.
One weak day doesn’t define your discipline.
And one person’s opinion doesn’t define your worth.

Sometimes we give one moment so much power that we forget everything else we’ve built, survived, and become.

Your life is bigger than what happened today. Keep the bigger picture in mind.
Send this to someone who needs motivation today 💪

Do you think India can become energy independent in the next 10 years?

In today’s episode, we sit down with Sumant Sinha - Founder, Chairman & CEO of @renewcorp one of the people who actually built India’s renewable energy industry from nothing.

Here’s what we discussed:
-Why Electricity Could Define the Future: Why electricity is only a part of the world’s total energy consumption and why electrification could reshape the energy industry.
-How China Dominated Clean Tech: How China built a major position across the global renewable energy and clean-tech supply chain.
-The AI Power Problem: Why the rapid growth of AI is creating huge electricity and grid demands, especially in countries with aging infrastructure.
-India’s Path to Energy Independence: What India would need to do over the next decade to become more energy independent.
-The Biggest Energy Bets for India: The three areas Sumant believes India should focus on to strengthen its energy future.
